newsitem.title: INDIA: Lightened Saudi jumbo jet takes off in Madras.
newsitem.headline: Lightened Saudi jumbo jet takes off in Madras.

text.p: A stripped-down Saudi Arabian Airlines jumbo jet that landed by mistake at an Indian military airfield took off safely on Friday from the compact runway where it made the screeching touch-down, officials said.

Turkish pilot Jam Joom used less than 4,000 feet (1,220 metres) of the 5,853-foot (1,784-metre) runway to lift the Boeing 747 into the air, and landed at Madras' commercial airport 10 minutes later, authorities said.

The Saudi jet had landed on Monday morning at the Tambaram Air Force airstrip instead of nearby Meenambakkam International Airport even though Indian defence officials fired red flares to warn the pilot against using the runway.

The pilot later told authorities he had mistaken the military airfield for the international airport although the commercial airstrip is more than twice as long as the 4,763-foot (1,452-metre) runway at Tambaram that he chose for landing.
None of the 331 passengers or 17 crew were hurt in Monday's landing, which one traveller called "rough and bumpy". The jumbo jet was on a flight from Dhahran in eastern Saudi Arabia to Madras.

Saudi and India officials, in consultation with Boeing Co, spent four days studying how to ensure a safe takeoff on a runway that was well short of the minimum 8,500 feet (2,591 metres) recommended for Boeing 747s.

To reduce weight, airline officials removed all galley equipment, toilet fittings and excess fuel, authorities said. Only two people other than the pilot were on board for the takeoff -- the co-pilot and flight engineer.
An air traffic controller at the military airport said the Turkish pilot made "a classic takeoff" before flying the jumbo jet to Madras airport, about 11 km (7 miles) away.
There the plane used more than 8,000 feet (2,440 metres) of the runway before coming to a halt.
Monday's freak landing was the latest in a series of potential air disasters in India.

Last month Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim said there had been 10 near-misses mainly involving commercial airliners in Indian airspace since the world's worst mid-air collision near New Delhi killed 349 people last November.
The Saudi captain was questioned earlier this week by Indian investigators, and two air traffic controllers at Madras airport were suspended pending completion of the inquiry.
Local newspapers said the radar at Madras airport was not working when the jumbo jet landed but other ground equipment was operating.
